results.title: Bi Chhus Theek, Doctor Sahib
results.description: The first kangri of the season had arrived in our OPD. It was tucked beneath the pheran of Ghulam Rasool sahib, a retired headmaster from Nowhatta, who walked in with his son, Bilal, close behind. “Salaam, Doctor sahib. Bi chhus theek,” he announced before he had even sat down. I am fine. Bilal had a different account. “He gets up four or five times every night. His pheran has become loose on him. Mouj says it is just the cold.” We asked Rasool sahib when he had last checked his blood sugar. “Shugar?” He laughed. “Doctor sahib, my father lived to ninety, eating two plates of bata twice a day. Nobody in our family ever had shugar.” Hat-hez soun khandaan Zaaneni ye Balai . We hear same version of this almost every week. Our fathers walked to the fields, the masjid and the market. Today, we eat much the same portions but spend far more time sitting- in cars, offices and in front of screens. The plate has stayed the same; the life around it has changed. We arranged an urgent assessment and a lab blood glucose. A finger-prick test took less than a minute. The glucometer showed 420 mg/dL, two hours after his breakfast of nun chai and two kulchas. “Khodayo,” Rasool sahib said quietly. After a pause, he added, “Yi chhu Khodaysund Karun .” This is God’s will. We hear that often, too. We told him what we tell our patients: faith also asks us to care for the body we have been given. Finding a health problem early is part of that care, not a challenge to it. Why early matters On 14 November, the world marks World Diabetes Day. The International Diabetes Federation’s theme for 2026 and 2027 is “Early action on diabetes”. The message is simple: identify the problem early, act in time and reduce the risk of complications. Rasool sahib’s thirst and frequent trips to the toilet at night were not the beginning of his diabetes; they were warning signs that had appeared late. Type 2 diabetes can remain silent for years. During that time, persistently high blood sugar can damage the eyes, kidneys and nerves, and increase the risk of heart and blood-vessel disease. Some of our patients discover they have diabetes only when they present with a foot wound that refuses to heal—or after a heart attack. “So all these years he had it, and we never knew?” Bilal asked. “Quite possibly.” “Then what about me?” That was the right question. The question every son and daughter should ask Bilal was 34. He worked at a bank desk and drove to the office. His waistline had gradually increased since his wedding, and his father’s diagnosis added another reason for him to get screened. People of South Asian origin are more likely to develop type 2 diabetes at a younger age and at a lower BMI than many other populations. A waist circumference above 90 cm in men or 80 cm in women is a warning sign—even when the weighing scale does not seem alarming. We advised Bilal to get a fasting blood glucose or HbA1c test. “Doctor sahib, I feel completely fine.” “So did your father, last year.” His report arrived two days later: HbA1c 6.1%. This was in the prediabetes range, not the diabetes range. “Wallah, so I have it?” “No. You have a warning sign—and the good news is that this is the stage when action can make a real difference.” Prediabetes is an important window of opportunity. At this stage, changes in eating habits, physical activity and weight can delay or, in some people, prevent the progression to type 2 diabetes. Large studies, including research from India, have demonstrated this. But taking action early matters. Nun chai, bata and the winter problem Then came the hard part: the kitchen. “You will stop my nun chai?” Rasool sahib asked, alarmed. “Nobody is taking your nun chai away,” we reassured him. The tea itself is not the main concern for blood sugar; it is often what accompanies it. Two kulchas, a bakarkhani or sometimes a butter-laden lavasa, repeated two or three times a day, followed by a full plate of bata at lunch and another at dinner. We agreed on small, realistic changes. One kulcha instead of two. Fill half the plate with haakh, nadru, dal or salad, and keep the portion of bata modest. Reduce the sugar in kehwa gradually, a little each week. At a wazwan, enjoy the rista and goshtaba, but be mindful of the rice and avoid making a second helping of phirin a habit. Winter brings its own challenge. Once Chillai Kalan sets in, many of us spend more time indoors, close to the kangri. Daily walking often falls away, and blood sugar control can suffer. We suggested that Rasool sahib begin with a 10–15-minute walk after meals—even indoors, or up and down the corridor if the weather is harsh. A short walk after eating can help reduce the rise in blood glucose. “Pakiv? At my age, Doctor sahib?” he asked with a smile. “Pakiv. Especially at your age.” ‘But I walk every day, Doctor sahib’ Before they left, Bilal waved in his mother, Mehmooda, who had been waiting on the bench outside. This was the same Mouj who had blamed the cold. She had a complaint of her own, and it came out in a rush.“Doctor sahib, I walk every morning, from our house to Jamia Masjid and back. I have stopped rice at night. I eat half of what I used to. And still my weight goes up. My sisters-in-law say I must be eating secretly.”She had gained six kilos in two years. Her knees ached on the stairs, Bilal said she snored, and her fasting sugar was close to the prediabetes range. We hear this frustration often, and it usually comes with a quieter shame: the feeling that the weighing scale is passing judgement on one’s character. So we told her what medical science now says plainly. Obesity is not a failure of willpower. It is a chronic disease. The body treats its stored fat as something to protect. When we eat less, the hormones that make us hungry rise and the hormones that tell us we are full fall. The body also starts burning fewer calories at rest, as if preparing for a famine. A morning walk is excellent for the heart, the blood sugar and the mood, but on its own it burns far less than most people imagine—roughly the energy in a single kulcha—and it often sharpens the appetite later in the day. Weight is also pushed upwards by poor sleep, stress, the hormonal changes around menopause, an underactive thyroid and some commonly used medicines, including steroids and certain drugs for depression, epilepsy and diabetes. And with every passing decade we lose muscle, the tissue that burns energy, unless we work to keep it. None of this means effort is wasted. It means obesity behaves like high blood pressure or diabetes itself: it has many causes, it tends to return when treatment stops, and it needs long-term care rather than a few weeks of starving. In 2025, both an international expert commission and a group of Indian experts, writing in The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology, moved towards judging obesity by what it is doing to a person’s health—the waist, blood sugar, blood pressure, joints, breathing during sleep—and not by the number on the scale alone. So we changed the question from “Why aren’t you trying harder?” to “What is driving your weight?” We checked her thyroid and HbA1c and went through every medicine she was taking. We kept the walk and added simple strength exercises twice a week—standing up from a chair and sitting down again, lifting water bottles filled at the tap—to protect her muscle. We moved some protein to breakfast: an egg, a bowl of curd or some dal alongside the nun chai, which keeps hunger away longer than a second kulcha. We talked about sleep. The first goal was simply to stop the gain; losing even five to ten per cent of body weight after that brings real benefits for sugar, blood pressure and knees. And we told her that if these steps were not enough, there are now effective medicines for obesity, and for some people surgery—prescribed and monitored by a doctor, not bought on a neighbour’s advice or after watching a video on the phone. “So it is not just me being greedy?” she asked. “No. It is a disease. And diseases are treated, not blamed.” What we do not say aloud At the door, Bilal lowered his voice. His younger sister had been unusually tired lately. Should she be tested, too? “But if anything is found, nobody should know. Her rishta is being discussed.”This is the part of diabetes we rarely discuss openly in Kashmir. Some families conceal the diagnosis, particularly in young women, fearing stigma and its consequences for marriage. That fear can delay testing and treatment. A woman whose diabetes is detected early and managed well can study, work, marry and have healthy children. It is delayed diagnosis and poor control—not the diagnosis itself—that can cause harm. A word, too, for parents: children can develop diabetes, most commonly type 1 diabetes. A child who suddenly becomes very thirsty, passes urine frequently, starts wetting the bed again or loses weight needs an urgent blood-glucose check. Type 1 diabetes can progress rapidly, and diabetic ketoacidosis can become life-threatening. Three months later Rasool sahib returned in February, through the snow, this time without his kangri. His blood sugars had improved. Bilal had lost a few centimetres around his waist and had started walking to work twice a week. Mehmooda’s weight had stopped climbing for the first time in years, and she had lost two kilos. “Doctor sahib,” Rasool sahib said as he sat down, “Bi chhus theek.” This time, we believed him. This World Diabetes Day, take one simple step. If you are 30 or older, have excess weight around your waist or have a family history of diabetes, get your blood sugar checked. A fasting blood glucose or HbA1c test is widely available at health centres. And if your weight keeps rising despite honest effort, see a doctor: that is a medical problem, not a moral one. Do not wait for excessive thirst or frequent urination. By then, the disease may have been present for years. Ghulam Rasool, Mehmooda and Bilal are composite characters based on everyday clinical encounters. Dr Muzaffar Amin Shah is Senior Resident and Dr M Hayat Bhat is Head Department of Endocrinology, GMC Srinagar
